candidates.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality
candidates.abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.

candidates.title: Newly Important Is Not Newly Built: What Reasoning Post-Training Adds Inside a Language Model, Why the Evidence Separates Representation From Wiring From Deployment, and the Cross-Model Tests That Would Show an Attention Head Is New
candidates.abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Reasoning models are built by post-training a pretrained model with supervised fine-tuning on teacher traces, with reinforcement learning against a verifier, or with both, and a running dispute asks whether this builds new machinery or redirects machinery the base model already had. A 2025 circuit study gave the first side a concrete form: attention heads that are absent from the base model's reasoning circuit and present after post-training, many of them after distillation and supervised fine-tuning, fewer and less stable after reinforcement learning. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that "new" has at least three separable meanings inside a model - a new representation, new wiring that consumes a representation, and a new policy for when existing behaviour is deployed - and that the measurements now in the record each speak to one of them. A head that enters a thresholded attribution circuit is newly important; whether it is newly built is a further question that the comparison as run cannot answer, because the reference model differs from the distilled model's actual parent, the circuit is defined by contrasting the two models' own response styles, and zero-ablation effects in the same study do not separate emergent heads from base-circuit heads or from heads taken from an unrelated task. The strongest cross-model evidence points to a regime split at the level of deployment: base-model steering vectors directed by the thinking model's own gating recover about 76% of the accuracy gap for reinforcement-learned models and about 11% for distilled ones, and a gap-matched pair computed from that study's table preserves the split. At the level of representation, a direction taken from the base model drives backtracking in a distilled model but not in the base. The paper consolidates these values in two tables and a figure, gives a classification procedure, and names five cross-model tests that would show whether a post-training head is new.

candidates.title: MAPS: Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning for Regulating Search Momentum in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by retrieving external knowledge. Recently, some RAG methods interleave reasoning and retrieval, enabling LLMs to progressively generate sub-queries and retrieve external knowledge. However, these methods may suffer from redundant or ineffective sub-queries and insufficiently diverse query exploration. Moreover, due to the tightly interleaved nature of reasoning and retrieval, it remains unclear how the evolving reasoning process influences query intent. To characterize the evolution of query intent during reasoning, we introduce search momentum, which captures the accumulated retrieval tendency induced by historical changes in generated sub-queries along the reasoning trajectory. Through momentum-based analysis, we find that the query generation process tends to continuously evolve along existing retrieval trajectories. Based on this observation, we propose MAPS, a Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning framework for regulating search momentum and mitigating query-intent drift. MAPS first retains the retrieved knowledge and a refined reasoning state, thereby reducing the influence of historical reasoning trajectories on subsequent sub-query generation. Subsequently, MAPS extends the conventional sequential reasoning process into a parallel reasoning paradigm. At each iteration, MAPS identifies complementary retrieval directions, generates corresponding sub-queries for parallel retrieval, and consolidates the retrieved evidence to update the knowledge and reasoning states. Experiments on six question-answering benchmarks demonstrate that MAPS consistently outperforms representative RAG methods across different backbone models. All code and resources are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/MAPS.

candidates.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. candidates.title: C$^2$U in RAG: Compositional Concept Unlearning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation can expose unwanted concepts through retrieved evidence even when the generator is moderated. We study query-side concept suppression with a fixed encoder and document index. Compositional Concept Unlearning (C$^2$U) routes a profile-derived direction through an augmented atom bank, adding only a bounded edited-minus-original delta to the raw query. Across five datasets, four encoders, and three seeds, the validation-selected configuration reduces pooled binary target Hit@5 by 4.25 percentage points with non-positive control degradation and target-exposure changes. Under the evaluated query transforms, it suppresses target density without increasing budgeted control-query exposure. Separately, ArXiv four-concept composition improves over an averaged-direction comparator after independent validation gates and first-use test evaluation.

candidates.title: NPUGen: NPU as KV Generator for Stable Long-Context Mobile LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: As on-device large language model (LLM) applications like mobile agents become increasingly popular, long-context inference has become a key challenge. The key-value (KV) cache is the foundation of efficient autoregressive decoding, but its memory footprint grows rapidly with context length, often exceeding the memory limits of mobile devices. Existing KV cache management methods, such as compression and storage offloading, often lead to performance degradation or unpredictable stall latency. We find that in the prevalent CPU/GPU-decoding mobile pipelines, the NPU remains largely idle during decoding and can recompute missing KV cache more efficiently than storage offloading. We therefore propose NPUGen, whose KV recomputation engine generates missing KV cache on the idle NPU via a prefill-like forward pass, avoiding unstable storage I/O, CPU intervention, and unnecessary data movement. NPUGen further introduces a hidden-state anchor mechanism that eliminates redundant prefix recomputation, and turns KV recomputation into a schedulable background service to cope with resource contention and guarantee foreground QoS. Experiments on smartphones with Qualcomm SoCs across multiple long-context tasks show that NPUGen significantly reduces decoding latency and fluctuations, providing fast and stable long-context inference on resource-constrained mobile devices.

candidates.title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose $\textbf{LongZero}$, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.

candidates.title: Post-Training Weight Quantization in Small Language Models: Reasoning–Efficiency Trade-offs Across GGUF Precision Levels
candidates.abstract: Weight quantization can reduce the storage and computational requirements of languagemodels, but it may also affect their reasoning capabilities. This study investigates whetherquantization causes gradual or abrupt degradation in the reasoning performance of smalllanguage models. Three instruction-tuned models were evaluated: Qwen3-0.6B, Gemma 3 1BIT, Llama 3.2 1B Instruct. Each model was tested using a BF16 reference version and fiveGGUF quantization formats: Q8_0, Q6_K, Q5_K_M, Q4_K_M and Q3_K_M.Evaluation was performed on the same fixed 50-question subset of the GSM8K mathematicalreasoning dataset. Exact-answer accuracy, average latency, peak RAM usage, generationspeed, and stored model size were recorded. The results show that quantization did notproduce one universal degradation pattern. Accuracy changes varied across models andprecision levels. Qwen Q4_K_M matched its BF16 accuracy, Gemma Q4_K_M recorded a numerically higher accuracy than BF16 in this pilot sample, 44% versus 42%; this small difference should not beinterpreted as evidence of a meaningful improvement, and Llama Q6_K achieved the highest quantized accuracy for that model. However, Q3_K_M produced larger accuracy reductions for Qwen and Llama.Quantization consistently improved storage and inference efficiency. These findings suggestthat quantization provides practical efficiency benefits, but the effect on reasoningperformance is model-dependent.Keywords: weight quantization; small language models; GGUF; reasoning; llama.cpp;inference efficiency, GSM8K

candidates.title: Parallel Thinking for Large Language Model with Path Diversity
candidates.abstract: Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exploring multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. However, we identify that parallel thinking via Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically suffers from the mode collapse of reasoning paths, where parallel thinking trajectories degenerate into similar ones. This homogeneity undermines the fundamental motivation of parallel thinking, that is, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking designed to encourage path diversity. DPT rewards the model to develop distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing the prefix similarity of parallel thinking paths, thereby enhancing a more comprehensive exploration of the reasoning space. We conduct various experiments and analyses across multiple reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of DPT. Results show that DPT successfully outperforms previous parallel thinking methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance over baselines. We validate path diversity as a key element to improve parallel thinking. Our code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/DPT.

candidates.title: Experimental reasoning in large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Scientific reasoning requires interaction with the physical world: designing experiments, interpreting outcomes, and deciding what experiment should come next. Here we show that general-purpose large language models (LLMs) already possess substantial capabilities for experimental reasoning. We connected LLMs to a liquid-handling robot and camera through PEARL, which provides perception, action, and persistent state. Given objectives rather than prescribed workflows, the system designed and successfully executed experiments, interpreted observations, and revised its approach as evidence accumulated. When information was insufficient, PEARL autonomously designed and performed intermediate experiments to acquire it. In quantitative enzyme characterization, it judged whether measurements were sufficient, new data were required, or conditions needed to change. Across eight scenarios, these behaviors were reliable with limited agent scaffolding and no supplied scenario-specific recovery recipes. More broadly, general-purpose LLMs may provide a reasoning layer between scientific objectives and physical experimentation, shifting laboratory automation from executing predefined procedures toward AI systems that participate directly in the experimental process.

candidates.title: Attention Sinks at Long Context: One Log-N Law for Retrieval and Abstention
candidates.abstract: Softmax attention cannot abstain on its own: its weights sum to one, so a head with nothing relevant to read must still attend somewhere. Trained models improvise such a place, the attention sink. Practice now builds one in: a null, an option that absorbs attention and delivers nothing, such as a learned sink logit, a register with zero value or an output gate. We show that these nulls are one mechanism, a gate on an ordinary softmax, and ask what happens to them as the context grows. The answer is one dilution law for two abilities. To retrieve, a matching key must outweigh the N other keys; to abstain when nothing matches, the null must. With bounded scores both leads must grow like log N, and because a query with a match and one without share the same null, no rule that sums over the keys keeps both at long context: a fixed null loses abstention, and a null that grows with the length loses retrieval. Tempering, which scales every score, the null included, by log N / log N_train, provably keeps both under margin conditions, and a head that decides by its largest score escapes the law. Trained heads in a controlled pilot follow the law closely, and tempering keeps both sides there, though not in every harder setting. In 125M-parameter language models, every rule with a null removed the first-token sink and most massive activations; past the training length, keeping positions in range mattered more than the null rule, and adding tempering to YaRN, which already includes a temperature, hurt. In small vision transformers trained at one resolution, tempering at evaluation raised accuracy at higher resolutions. A prespecified test on gpt-oss was inconclusive. This is a working draft, not a final version. It is unpolished in places, incomplete in others, and keeps exploratory material a polished paper would leave out, because that material helps decide what comes next and shows the programme's big picture more fully. Please read it with that in mind: the work will be refined further, and later versions will appear under this record. It belongs to a collection released together on Zenodo: the entry paper The Transformer Abides, the monograph A Spectral Theory of Token Communication, and the papers Attention Sinks at Long Context, The Transformer as a Constrained Equilibrium and Beyond Transformers. This version is the text; the records, the code and the formal proofs follow in a later version.

candidates.title: RISK-KV: Quality-Aware Selective KV Cache Reconstruction for Distributed LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Request migration and interruption recovery in distributed large language model (LLM) inference rely on historical key-value (KV) caches. Retaining or transferring a complete cache incurs substantial state overhead, whereas replaying historical tokens requires additional computation. This paper proposes RISK-KV, a quality-aware method for selective historical KV reconstruction in pretrained models. RISK-KV uses exact KV states on both sides of a target layer and cross-layer ridge regression to predict the missing layer's attention-projection input; it then folds in the original model's KV projection matrices to reduce predictor storage. Reconstruction risk is measured by the change in negative log-likelihood (NLL) caused by actual reconstruction, and low-overhead topology search with quality gating selects the layer groups to reconstruct. Independent tests on three language models show that representative recovery configurations omit 18.2 percent to 33.3 percent of historical KV, with perplexity changes below 0.5 percent. In a local request-recovery experiment with a 512-token history, RISK-KV achieves a 1.51 to 3.31 times speedup over full Token Replay. These results indicate that selective KV reconstruction can reduce historical cache overhead with small changes in predictive quality and improve request-recovery efficiency under the evaluated deployment conditions.

candidates.title: Prism : Efficient Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning for On-Device LLMs
candidates.abstract: On-device fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming increasingly important for personalized AI assistants and adaptive agents. However, standard backpropagation imposes substantial training-state memory overheads that often exceed the stringent resource budgets of mobile platforms. To address this, Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization leverages forward-only probing instead of backpropagation, drastically reducing memory footprints and offering a compelling alternative for on-device adaptation. Nonetheless, scaling ZO fine-tuning to billion-scale trainable parameter spaces remains challenging, as the cost of recovering reliable update directions scales poorly with dimensionality under mobile constraints. In this paper, we present Prism, a mobile-native infrastructure for practical billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning. Prism re-architects the ZO loop around a scalable probing substrate, bringing both per-step training latency and memory overhead closer to the inference footprint. We implement Prism end to end on commodity smartphones and evaluate it across diverse tasks and multiple model scales. Prism achieves accuracy comparable to that of state-of-the-art ZO fine-tuning baselines while reducing per-step latency by 53.4%-76.3% and peak memory by 10.6%-13.8% relative to the best baseline in each setting. These results demonstrate the practical feasibility of billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning for LLMs under real mobile constraints. We will release our code to support future research.

candidates.title: Human Oversight for LLM-Assisted Clinical Documentation
candidates.abstract: Clinical documentation is essential to healthcare delivery but is timeconsuming, cognitively demanding, and prone to error. Large language models (LLMs) can generate draft notes, but may introduce hallucinations, unsupported inferences, or factual distortions that clinicians overlook. This study evaluated whether transparency features improve clinician oversight in LLM-assisted documentation. Using a crossover design, 40 clinicians reviewed AI-generated notes under three conditions: a standard LLM interface, token-level uncertainty highlighting, and uncertainty highlighting combined with direct links to electronic medical record fields. Outcomes included factual errors remaining in finalized notes, editing time, trust, perceived control, and cognitive load. The combined uncertainty-plus-source-link interface performed best, reducing factual errors by 41% and editing time by 18% compared with the standard condition. Uncertainty highlighting alone offered partial benefits but still required manual record verification. These findings indicate that LLM-assisted documentation is safer and more efficient when transparency features support verification, direct attention, and preserve clinician control.

candidates.title: HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts. To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed directly without additional data rearrangement while maintaining transfer efficiency. We implement and evaluate HAWK on a system built with commercially available GPUs and NPUs, demonstrating performance within 7.88% of a GPU-only system under the same SLO constraints while achieving up to 1.26$\times$ higher power efficiency and 1.72$\times$ higher cost efficiency.

candidates.title: From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied across the scientific discovery pipeline, from synthesizing literature to generating hypotheses to informing experimental design. A unifying principle behind these tasks is the need to continuously update beliefs as evidence accumulates, for which Bayesian inference provides a natural framework. However, existing work assumes that LLMs cannot carry out principled Bayesian belief updating in context, instead relying on simplifications and heuristics. To challenge this assumption, we present a principled evaluation of Bayesian reasoning capabilities in LLMs, analyzing both the model's internal consistency as well as its ability to recover an externally determined posterior. Specifically, we build an evaluation framework spanning qualitative epistemological examples to probe probabilistic coherence, quantitative benchmarks of Bayesian inference capabilities, and analyses of the impact of non-Bayesian updates on downstream task performance. Across different scenarios, we find that LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating their beliefs in context. However, when equipped with modern reasoning abilities and code execution capabilities, their performance drastically improves, enabling even the close approximation of analytically intractable posteriors. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs with access to appropriate tools could already be used to make complex belief updates in scientific discovery, enabling rapid acceleration of the efficiency and scale of AI-powered scientific discovery.

candidates.title: Networked trust-game data for "Does social networking agency shape trust and reciprocity similarly in large language model agents and humans?"
candidates.abstract: This dataset supports the manuscript “Does social networking agency shape trust and reciprocity similarly in large language model agents and humans?” The archive contains recorded decisions and generated responses from large language model (LLM) agents in a networked trust game, together with executed allocation tables, prompts, synthetic personas and archived experiment configurations. The main experiments comprise three sessions for each of five nominal proportions of free agents (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1). Each session includes 49 agents on a periodic 7 × 7 lattice with four neighbours and lasts 20 rounds. Each agent acts as both trustor and trustee in each round. Free trustors may differentiate investments across neighbours, whereas constrained trustors allocate equally. The three CSV exports contain 14,700 agent-round records in total. A separate exploratory dataset contains one 20-round session per nominal proportion. These sessions used a different instruction concerning terminal-round assumptions and should not be pooled with the main experiments as repetitions of the same protocol. The included README provides the directory structure, experimental conditions, JSON schema, CSV data dictionary and guidance for reuse. Behavioural analyses of the main experiments should use the executed allocations rather than assume that allocations stated in generated text were executed unchanged. Amounts and payoffs are expressed in experimental tokens, not currency. Human benchmark data are not included. They originate from Jia et al. (2025), “Social networking agency and prosociality are inextricably linked in economic games” (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02289-0), and are available from the original authors’ project at https://osf.io/n84dv/. candidates.title: HalluciGuard-eye: knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation for hallucination detection and mitigation in ophthalmic multimodal large language models
candidates.abstract: Background Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults, yet scalable early detection is limited by the unreliability of AI-assisted screening. Multimodal large language models can interpret fundus photographs and support DR grading, but they frequently hallucinate - fabricating lesions or misclassifying referable DR - which directly threatens timely treatment and prevention of vision loss. We developed HalluciGuard-Eye to make AI-assisted DR assessment trustworthy. Methods HalluciGuard-Eye combines knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation with hierarchical hallucination detection. An Ophthalmic Clinical Knowledge Graph containing 47,832 medical entities and 156,294 semantic relationships was constructed from clinical guidelines and published literature. A dual-stream architecture uses a Visual-Semantic Alignment Module to verify cross-modal consistency and a Clinical Factuality Grounding Network to anchor generated content to reranked evidence. The Hierarchical Factuality Score assesses anatomical, pathological, and clinical-recommendation accuracy. The framework was evaluated on four public ophthalmic imaging benchmarks. Results HalluciGuard-Eye reduced hallucination rates by 42.2% compared with state-of-the-art medical multimodal large language models and achieved 91.6% factual accuracy for clinical entity recognition on EyePACS. For diabetic retinopathy grading, sensitivity was 89.6% and specificity was 92.1%, representing improvements of 2.4% and 2.7%, respectively, over MedRAG. In the component ablation, removing knowledge-graph retrieval lowered EyePACS HFS by 9.4 percentage points. Additional analyses yielded 87.6% critical-evidence recall@20, 89.2% lesion-location accuracy, and 88.9% sensitivity in a patient-clustered cohort. Conclusions These results indicate that knowledge-grounded retrieval and hierarchical factuality assessment can reduce hallucinations while preserving diagnostic performance in ophthalmic multimodal language models.

candidates.title: Comparative Analysis of Transformer Models for Prompt Injection Detection in Autonomous Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a significant security challenge for large language model systems, particularly autonomous large language model-based agents that may interact with external tools, application programming interfaces, and data sources.This study presents a comparative evaluation of five pre-trained transformer models, namely BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, DistilBERT, and ALBERT, fine-tuned for binary prompt injection classification.A balanced dataset of 4,224 samples was compiled from 10 publicly accessible corpora containing benign and injection prompts and divided into training (2,956), validation (634), and test (634) sets.The models were trained in the Kaggle environment using an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, the AdamW optimizer, and a linear warm-up scheduling strategy.On the held-out test set, RoBERTa achieved the highest classification performance, with 97.48% accuracy, 97.52% macro-precision, 97.48% macro-recall, 97.48% macro-F1-score, and 99.64% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.DistilBERT achieved the highest reported throughput of 819.13 samples/s and the lowest per-sample latency of 1.22 ms.Statistical analysis using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and SHapley Additive exPlanations-based interpretability analysis were also conducted to examine model differences and influential linguistic features.The findings demonstrate that fine-tuned transformer classifiers can achieve strong performance on the evaluated benchmark dataset while exhibiting different accuracyefficiency characteristics.However, the results should be interpreted within the scope of the evaluated data distribution, as the study does not include independent external datasets or adaptive adversarial attacks.These limitations indicate that further validation is required to establish generalizability and robustness in real-world prompt-injection defense scenarios.

candidates.title: Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over Federated Cloud Data Lakes
candidates.abstract: Abstract: Enterprise deployments of large language models require grounding generated answers in authoritative, continuously updated internal repositories while strictly enforcing row- and document-level access control lists (ACLs). Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines that chunk PDF documents into fixed 500-token windows and execute unconstrained approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) vector searches fail in production across three dimensions: they lose cross-section structural context in complex financial and technical tables, they suffer lexical blindness on exact product codes and regulatory statutes, and they leak unauthorized knowledge when ACL filtering is applied post-retrieval. This paper presents a federated Enterprise RAG architecture spanning cloud data lakes (Apache Iceberg on AWS S3, Snowflake, and Google BigQuery). Building on foundational RAG formulations (Lewis et al., 2020), ColBERT late-interaction retrieval (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020), and GraphRAG hierarchical community indexing (Edge et al., 2024), our architecture combines layout-aware semantic chunking, contextual header injection, three-way hybrid retrieval (dense HNSW vectors + BM25s sparse lexical + entity knowledge graph traversal) fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al., 2009), cross-encoder reranking, and cryptographic pre-retrieval ACL bitmap filtering. We evaluate the architecture through a production case study modeled on Morgan Stanley Wealth Management knowledge assistants and Ramp automated financial document analysis pipelines over a 14.8-million-document federated corpus. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that hybrid ACL-aware RAG increases Context Recall@10 from 61.2% (dense-only baseline) to 93.4%, raises RAGAS Faithfulness from 0.74 to 0.96, reduces hallucinated ungrounded claims from 14.8% to 1.2%, and enforces zero unauthorized document leakage at a P95 end-to-end retrieval latency of 168 milliseconds. Research Domain & Specialization Track Master of Science in Information Technology (MSIT) — Information Retrieval, Enterprise Generative AI, and Cloud Data Lakes. Core Technical Highlights Empirical Production Case Studies: Rigorous architectural blueprints and telemetry evaluation across enterprise cloud deployments. Four-Tier Reference Architecture: Formal specification from edge ingress to distributed hardware execution pools. Mathematical Formulation: Formally derived algorithmic and optimization models with closed-loop verification. Multi-Modal Benchmarking: Comparative empirical baselines under fault-injection and synthetic workload scaling. candidates.title: Projected-Feature Scale Calibration for 2-Bit Vision Encoders in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Very low-bit quantization of a multimodal large language model’s vision encoder can impair text recognition and chart understanding. We present projected-feature scale calibration (PSC), an image-only post-training method for 2-bit vision encoders. PSC starts from range-searched GPTQ, fixes integer codes and zero points, and jointly updates existing group scales by matching features through a frozen multimodal projector. This objective aligns image-only calibration with the visual representation supplied to the language model. The learned updates fold directly into the original scales, preserving the inference architecture. Experiments on LLaVA-OneVision show consistent improvements in text recognition and chart understanding over the same strong quantized initialization, including under simultaneous language-model compression. Matched controls support projected-feature supervision over encoder-output reconstruction, repeated calibration samples confirm stable gains, and an unchanged-recipe contrastive language–image pre-training (CLIP) evaluation supports transfer to a second encoder. PSC thus improves the accuracy of compact vision encoders while preserving their quantized representation.

candidates.title: Building a Nested LADDER for LLM Unstructured Post-Training Pruning
candidates.abstract: Non-uniform allocation can improve post-training pruning of large language models, yet quality can still degrade sharply at high sparsity. To control degradation as sparsity increases, we introduce LADDER (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement), which allocates sparsity incrementally. At each step, it evaluates pruning an additional fraction of weights from each eligible layer and commits the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter. This process produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple budgets. We evaluate LADDER on five OPT, Llama, and Qwen models across 10-90% sparsity, using SparseGPT as its candidate-generation backend and comparing against uniform and adaptive allocation baselines. Results reveal a clear operating-regime trade-off: LADDER is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity but becomes substantially more robust from 70% onward. This high-sparsity advantage largely persists after posterior distillation across four of five models and translates into improved retention of aggregate zero-shot accuracy.

candidates.title: Adaptive Stopping of Streamed Reasoning for Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Reasoning-enabled language model agents can incur substantial computation before acting, although the reasoning needed varies across decisions. Existing stopping signals, such as confidence and intermediate-answer stability, can vary in effectiveness across reasoning models; signals obtained from hidden states or token probabilities also require internal access that may be unavailable or impractical. We introduce StreamStop, which learns model-specific stopping policies offline from prefix-level action agreement. A frozen prefix reader encodes available reasoning text for a lightweight stop head, allowing stopping without access to the reasoning model's internal signals. We construct and publicly release a dataset of agent reasoning trajectories with prefix-level action annotations. These annotations compare each prefix action with the full-reasoning reference action, enabling offline comparison of stopping rules and exact expected-return optimization of a discounted action-agreement objective. Conditioning the head on the discount factor allows the agreement-token trade-off to be adjusted at inference without retraining. In closed-loop evaluations on WebShop and ScienceWorld, StreamStop achieves higher observed success than most validation-selected fixed-budget settings while using fewer reasoning tokens than Full thinking. On WebShop with Qwen3.8-27B, it uses 42% fewer reasoning tokens per episode with similar observed task success.

candidates.title: Local Inference of LLMs on Long Contexts: A Data Systems Perspective
candidates.abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.

candidates.title: Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Tactile Multimodal Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Tactile Perception, Reasoning, Generation, and Physical Feedback
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have expanded artificial intelligence beyond text to include visual and auditory information. However, tactile interaction remains comparatively fragmented across sensing hardware, haptic signal interpretation, tactile generation, and device-specific feedback mechanisms. This paper proposes Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Tactile Multimodal Intelligence (SBTMI), a conceptual framework for integrating tactile input and physical tactile output into smartphone-centered multimodal large language model systems. Unlike approaches that focus exclusively on tactile classification, tactile captioning, or the generation of haptic effects from textual descriptions, the proposed framework organizes tactile perception, semantic reasoning, tactile generation, physical actuation, and feedback-based adaptation within a unified interaction architecture. The framework consists of five principal components: a tactile acquisition interface, a tactile representation module, a multimodal reasoning controller, a tactile generation module, and a device-specific actuation interface. A closed-loop interaction mechanism enables the system to compare intended tactile effects with subsequent sensor observations and adjust its outputs accordingly. The framework distinguishes native smartphone capabilities from capabilities requiring external tactile sensors or actuators. We formulate research questions, define optimization objectives and evaluation metrics, and propose experiments for assessing tactile understanding, generation quality, cross-modal consistency, latency, robustness, and closed-loop performance. This work is a conceptual research proposal rather than an empirically validated system. Its contribution is a unified architectural and experimental framework for investigating bidirectional tactile intelligence in smartphone-centered multimodal AI.

candidates.title: Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Pain-Related Multimodal Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Pain Sensing, Contextual Reasoning, Safe Sensory Feedback, and Adaptive Interaction
candidates.abstract: Pain is a complex sensory and affective experience that is difficult to measure objectively and cannot be reduced to a single physiological signal. Smartphones and wearable devices have already been used to collect pain reports, monitor physiological correlates, and support pain assessment. Separately, artificial nociceptive systems and sensory-feedback interfaces have investigated how machines can detect potentially harmful stimuli and communicate information through physical feedback. However, the integration of pain-related sensing, multimodal large language model reasoning, and safe, bidirectional sensory interaction within a smartphone-centered architecture remains a research question requiring systematic investigation. This paper proposes Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Pain-Related Multimodal Large Language Models (SBP-MLLMs), a conceptual framework for integrating pain-related input and controlled sensory feedback with multimodal reasoning. The architecture includes a smartphone host, a pain-related data acquisition interface, a multimodal representation encoder, a contextual reasoning controller, a safety-constrained feedback planner, and an output interface. The input pathway combines voluntary pain reports with available physiological, behavioral, and contextual information, while explicitly distinguishing measured signals from subjective pain experience. The output pathway communicates pain-related information through visual, auditory, vibrotactile, or other validated non-injurious feedback. Where clinically justified, specialized external devices may be considered under appropriate professional oversight, but the proposed framework does not require deliberately inducing pain. A closed-loop controller compares intended feedback with observed user responses and device status, while respecting consent and safety constraints. The paper formalizes the architecture, identifies research questions, and proposes an experimental evaluation protocol. The framework is conceptual and has not been experimentally validated. Its potential contribution is the integration of pain-related perception, multimodal reasoning, and safe bidirectional interaction rather than the invention of pain sensing, pain monitoring, or sensory stimulation.

candidates.title: Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Olfactory Multimodal Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Smell Sensing, Semantic Reasoning, Scent Generation, and Closed-Loop Olfactory Interaction
candidates.abstract: Human–computer interaction has primarily relied on visual, auditory, and tactile channels, while olfaction remains comparatively underrepresented in general-purpose mobile computing. Recent advances in electronic noses, smartphone-connected gas sensors, artificial intelligence-based scent creation, and wearable olfactory displays provide important foundations for integrating smell into digital systems. However, a unified architecture in which a smartphone-centered multimodal large language model coordinates olfactory input, semantic interpretation, context-dependent scent generation, and feedback-based correction remains a research direction requiring systematic investigation. This paper proposes Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Olfactory Multimodal Large Language Models (SBOM-LLMs), a conceptual framework that integrates olfactory sensing and physical scent output with multimodal large language model reasoning. The proposed architecture consists of six components: a smartphone host, an olfactory acquisition interface, an olfactory representation encoder, a multimodal reasoning controller, a constrained scent-generation planner, and a physical olfactory output interface. The framework supports two complementary capabilities: translating environmental odor measurements into machine-interpretable semantic representations and translating multimodal intentions into controlled physical scent outputs. A closed-loop mechanism compares intended scent specifications with sensor measurements and available delivery telemetry, enabling iterative adjustment when appropriate. The paper formalizes the architecture, defines candidate optimization objectives, proposes an experimental evaluation protocol, and discusses safety, calibration, personalization, and hardware constraints. This work presents a conceptual research framework rather than a validated implementation. Its potential contribution lies in the integration and coordination of existing olfactory technologies with general-purpose multimodal reasoning, not in claiming to invent electronic noses or digital scent displays.

candidates.title: Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Gustatory Multimodal Large Language Models: A Unified Framework for Taste Sensing, Reasoning, Generation, and Physical Taste Feedback
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly integrate text, images, and audio, yet taste remains an underrepresented modality in smartphone-centered artificial intelligence. Existing research has developed electronic tongues, portable taste interfaces, digital taste stimulation, and sensor–actuator systems for remote tasting. However, the integration of these capabilities into a unified smartphone-centered multimodal large language model presents additional research questions concerning sensory representation, semantic reasoning, taste generation, device control, and feedback-based adaptation. This paper proposes Smartphone-Native Bidirectional Gustatory Intelligence (SNBGI), a conceptual framework that connects gustatory input and gustatory output through a common multimodal reasoning architecture. The proposed system receives taste-related chemical measurements from electronic-tongue sensors or compatible sensing peripherals, interprets these observations in context, generates structured gustatory output specifications, and communicates with a device capable of producing controlled taste stimuli. A closed-loop mechanism enables the system to compare intended taste profiles with subsequent sensor measurements and user feedback. The framework distinguishes objective chemical sensing from subjective human taste perception and distinguishes smartphone software from the external hardware required for physical taste stimulation. We formulate research questions, mathematical objectives, implementation components, and an experimental protocol for evaluating taste classification, generation accuracy, perceptual correspondence, response latency, portability, and safety. The contribution is a proposed architecture and validation program, not a claim that digital taste sensing or generation has been invented for the first time. The framework aims to provide a foundation for investigating how smartphone-based multimodal AI can perceive, reason about, and generate taste-related experiences.

candidates.title: PI-MLLM: Psychophysics-Inspired Multimodal Large Language Model for Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis
candidates.abstract: Oddly Satisfying Videos (OSVs) can evoke strong viewer responses through repetitive motion, visual tactility, and ASMR-like sounds despite containing few explicit semantic emotion cues. This makes OSVs a challenging setting for Video Emotion Analysis (VEA), since most existing methods focus on semantic video content and under-model the physical sensory dynamics that shape viewer responses. To support Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis (OSVEA), we construct the Oddly Satisfying Video Dataset (OSVD), comprising 12,000 annotated 5-second clips. Each clip provides viewer-emotion labels under video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual conditions, together with explanations grounded in visual and acoustic sensory evidence. Building on OSVD, we propose PI-MLLM, a psychophysics-inspired multimodal large language model that integrates Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment (MSDA) and Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution (CAVA). MSDA uses auxiliary prediction objectives to align modality representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics. CAVA evaluates emotion scores across modality coalitions and applies Shapley attribution to identify the dominant modality and determine whether visual and auditory evidence is synergistic or conflicting. Experiments show that PI-MLLM improves both viewer-side emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality, suggesting the value of physical sensory cues to video emotion analysis.

candidates.title: Language Impairment as a Lens onto Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) encode language in highly distributed spaces, they remain vulnerable to focal disruptions---a phenomenon strikingly similar to how localized brain damage causes clinical aphasia in humans. To investigate this theoretical tension, we ask whether LLMs possess a functional structure analogous to the human language system, by introducing a novel mechanistic interpretability framework inspired by aphasia. Through two complementary approaches, classifier-guided lesioning and continuous activation steering, we systematically induce aphasia-like breakdowns in LLMs. We find that language functions can be successfully isolated to discrete structural circuits and continuous representational vectors, yet these functions remain densely entangled with significant circuit overlap and vector similarities across distinct aphasic profiles. Furthermore, while steering generalizes robustly across downstream tasks, structural lesioning remains asymmetrically constrained. By bridging neuropsychology and mechanistic interpretability, we demonstrate that LLMs, functionally analogous to biological brains, rely on a densely entangled architecture that can be systematically mapped through clinically-informed interventions.

candidates.title: Imagination or Reason? A Spinozist Criterion for Genuine Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: When Webb, Holyoak, and Lu reported that large language models (LLMs) solve a wide range of analogy problems zero-shot, they reopened an old philosophical question: do such systems reason relationally, or do they exploit surface regularities absorbed from training? Critics show that performance degrades on counterfactual variants that leave human performance intact; defenders answer that these failures reflect peripheral deficits. I argue that the debate lacks a principled criterion for distinguishing genuine relational reasoning from associative pattern-completion, and that Spinoza’s epistemology supplies one. Spinoza separates imagination—general ideas formed through the contingent order in which the body is affected—from reason, the adequate cognition of what is genuinely common through common notions; his own illustration (Ethics 2p40s2) is a proportional analogy that turns on the difference between applying a learned rule and grasping a common form. Reconstructed functionally, the distinction yields a diagnostic heuristic: invariance of competence under transformations that preserve relational structure while destroying surface similarity counts as defeasible evidence of relational grounding. This separates the following two questions the literature conflates: whether a system produces correct analogies, and whether its competence is relationally grounded. I give the criterion a measurement protocol and apply it symmetrically to humans and machines.

candidates.title: Hidden Messages Between Diffusion Language Model Agents: Causal Evidence for Latent Communication
candidates.abstract: Diffusion language models form answers through a sequence of revisable continuous states, but multi-agent systems usually discard those states and make agents communicate only after decoding text. We ask whether one independent diffusion trajectory can pass a compact hidden message into another and, crucially, whether the receiver uses what that message means. In Hidden Messages, a sender compresses its denoising state into four signed dense vectors; the receiver consumes them while retaining its own context, canvas, and trajectory. Removing a message tests whether the channel matters; replacing it with a message from another example tests whether its content matters. Across controlled tasks, derangement removes a +63.6-point advantage on Tiny-A2D and a +100.0-point advantage on Dream-7B, while targeted substitutions steer the receiver toward the substituted fact. On QASC with the two supporting facts split across agents, matched communication reaches 80.8%, but a wrong-example message lowers accuracy to 46.8%, a content effect of +34.0 points. The surprising result is temporal: one late transfer reaches 87.8%, exceeding four recurrent exchanges by +7.0 points. These experiments provide causal evidence for continuous hidden communication between diffusion-LM agents and show that when information is transferred can matter more than how many times agents exchange it.

candidates.title: Fundamentals of Natural Language Processing and Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This chapter introduces the fundamental principles of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs) within the context of Sports Science and data-driven analytics. It demonstrates how unstructured textual and vocal data complement traditional numerical performance metrics by capturing contextual, psychological, and communicative aspects of sport environments. The chapter systematically presents core NLP techniques, including tokenization, lemmatization, sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, topic modeling, and word embeddings, and explains their role in transforming language-based data into structured representations for performance analysis and decision-making. Building on these foundations, the chapter examines key neural network architectures used in NLP, particularly recurrent neural networks, Long Short-Term Memory models, and Transformer-based systems. Special emphasis is placed on the attention mechanism and its role in enabling scalable and context-aware language modelling. The chapter further analyzes the capabilities and limitations of Large Language Models, including their generative potential, adaptability through fine-tuning and prompt-based interaction, and challenges such as hallucinations, bias, and interpretability. Through multimodal integration and applied case studies, the chapter highlights how NLP and LLMs contribute to sports analytics, athlete monitoring, talent identification, and real-time decision-making.

candidates.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

candidates.title: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Industrial Cybersecurity Compliance Assessment
candidates.abstract: This paper presents a methodology for evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in industrial cybersecurity compliance assessment. The study focuses on whether AI-generated compliance judgments are supported by authoritative cybersecurity guidance and evidence of control implementation. The proposed evaluation uses NIST Special Publication 800-82 Revision 3 as its primary reference source and defines three assessment outcomes: compliant, non-compliant, and insufficient evidence. The planned benchmark examines five evidence conditions: full supporting evidence, partial supporting evidence, irrelevant evidence, absent evidence, and contradictory evidence. The methodology describes a human annotation and adjudication process and proposes metrics for classification performance, retrieval relevance, evidence grounding, citation correctness, and uncertainty handling. This manuscript is a methodology-focused research preprint. The full benchmark experiments and quantitative evaluation have not been completed, and no empirical performance claims are made. Further dataset construction, experimental execution, and independent evaluation are required.

candidates.title: Collaborative reasoning framework integrating multimodal large language models and knowledge graphs for dragon and lion dance technical action semantic understanding
candidates.abstract: Dragon and lion dance occupies an unusual position: a nationally recognised item of intangible cultural heritage that is at the same time a codified competitive sport. Judging it is correspondingly hard, because one scored element carries temporal, spatial, dynamic and cooperative meaning at once. This study couples a multimodal large language model (MLLM) with a domain-specific knowledge graph (KG) so that technical actions can be recognised, scored and explained against the rulebook. The graph encodes 100 action types, 224 technical elements, 135 scoring criteria and 83 common error patterns, all distilled from official regulations, expert interviews and historical competition records. A perception-retrieval-reasoning pipeline drives the framework: the MLLM proposes a preliminary label, that label triggers structured subgraph retrieval, and the retrieved triples then constrain multi-hop reasoning. A cross-modal anchoring module aligns visual action embeddings with KG entity representations through contrastive learning with rule-aware hard negatives, while a path verbaliser converts the winning traversal into a rule-referenced adjudication report. We evaluate on 4,659 clips split disjointly by competition, so that no routine, team or venue appears in more than one subset. Measured against skeleton-based recognisers, recent video MLLMs, graph-augmented retrieval pipelines and a dedicated action quality assessment regressor, the framework reaches 82.7% classification accuracy, 44.2 BLEU-4 and 61.5 ROUGE-L; it predicts execution scores with a Spearman correlation of 0.812 and a relative L2 distance of 0.681, identifies deduction items at 79.4% F1, and cites the correct rule clause 85.6% of the time. Ablations, hyper-parameter sweeps, efficiency profiling and degraded-video tests indicate that knowledge grounding, perceptual anchoring, structured explanation and conflict-driven re-retrieval each address a different failure mode. Two clips traced end to end, one handled correctly and one not, show that every sentence of a generated report maps onto a graph edge that a reviewer can inspect. The framework is offered as a design for adjudication support that informs a judging panel rather than replacing it; whether it transfers to sports governed by other rulebooks has yet to be tested.

candidates.title: Chart Reasoning with Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Chart reasoning requires multimodal models to interpret visual encodings, derive structured semantics, execute formal reasoning procedures, and generate evidence-grounded outputs. This survey reviews chart reasoning methodologies for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), categorizing them by their primary intervention points: data and supervision design, inference-time reasoning strategies, and model-integrated optimization. We examine how existing approaches extract chart semantics, use intermediate representations, execute reasoning workflows, ground predictions in visual evidence, and verify outputs. We also summarize major chart reasoning benchmarks and cross-paradigm empirical results, and examine limitations in current evaluation protocols and metrics. Finally, we discuss recurring challenges in synthetic-to-real generalization, semantic reconstruction, visual grounding, reasoning faithfulness, and diagnostic evaluation, outlining directions toward more reliable and generalizable chart reasoning systems.

candidates.title: Chapter 37: Large language models
candidates.abstract: Machine learning for text data has undergone a revolution with the emergence of deep neural networks based on the transformer architecture. The term large language model (LLM) nowadays implies such neural networks, with some models exceeding a trillion parameters. LLMs are also used for nontext data, including music, images, video, and even scientific data like protein sequences. Multiple modalities, e.g., image and text, can also be combined easily. This chapter presents the main features of a transformer neural network for predicting the next word (or token ) of an input sequence of words. An example of such a neural network is the now-classical Generative Pretrained Transformer 3, or GPT-3, for which there is ample public information. 21 LLMs are a rapidly advancing field, but what you learn here should give you a fundamental understanding for exploring state-of-the-art language models in research papers and other resources. 21 Our presentation is inspired by [Richard E. Turner, An Introduction to Transformers , preprint, arXiv:2304.10557 [cs.LG], 2026], and [Mary Phuong and Marcus Hutter, Formal Algorithms for Transformers , preprint, arXiv:2207.09238 [cs.LG], 2022].

candidates.title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.

candidates.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.

candidates.title: AgenticRoboRL: Bringing Coding-Agent Post-Training to Agentic Robotics
candidates.abstract: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.

candidates.title: Value-level data provenance in an electronic laboratory notebook used by humans and language-model agents: An experience report
candidates.abstract: A published laboratory number can be verified only when its raw file and extraction method are known. This paper presents the value-level provenance architecture of APS ELN, an electronic laboratory notebook used by both researchers and language-model agents. The architecture was motivated by a production audit in a materials laboratory covering projects performed over almost 5 years. Tracing eight baseline studies from sample to stored value showed that the initial ELN structure preserved the link from sample to raw file. Still, the link from raw file to stored value was lost, mainly due to human factors: manual entries carried no file reference or extractor version. To close this gap, the database design and workflow were reworked so that every stored value records its source file, the data file reader/viewer (DFR) plugin and version, any interactive analysis selection, or the server-side formula for derived quantities. An automated drift check re-runs each DFR on the stored files. In two end-to-end validation studies recorded by agents in X-ray reflectivity and tribology, all stored values retained verifiable provenance with zero drift. A comparison with five other platforms shows that none binds individual stored numbers to both their source files and extractor versions.

candidates.title: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings
candidates.abstract: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings. Evaluations on graph-theoretic benchmarks also show that performance on small graphs is preserved.

candidates.title: Reasoning as a Distribution: Generative Plan Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
candidates.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable: without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled (coverage), selected on request (steering), and reweighted by deployment outcomes (outcome adaptation). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with $π_0$, and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.

candidates.title: Auditing Conformal Prediction for Language Models Under Inference-Time Model Shift
candidates.abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) for language models is typically evaluated under a matched protocol, in which calibration and deployment use the same post-training inference configuration, such as quantization mode and inference temperature. In deployment, these choices often differ from those used at calibration to meet memory or throughput constraints or serving policies. We argue that this exposes a limitation in current CP evaluation protocols for language models. We formalize the underlying phenomenon as inference-time model shift: a change in the conformal score distribution induced by inference configuration rather than by the input--label distribution, and theoretically characterize how it breaks split-conformal exchangeability even when the task distribution and trained model are unchanged. We then evaluate its consequences across 8 language models, 4 finite-label benchmarks, and 12 inference configurations. We find that matched evaluation can substantially overstate deployment-time coverage, and that the effect is heterogeneous across models and datasets. We argue that inference configuration should be reported as a first-class experimental axis in CP evaluations for language-model systems.

candidates.title: Enhancing Large Language Models Through Pre-Training, In-Training, and Post-Training Deletion
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly enhanced through additional data, parameter optimization, architectural modifications, preference optimization, and increased computational resources. However, improvement does not necessarily require adding information, parameters, components, or computational operations. In some circumstances, the removal of selected objects may improve a model by reducing redundancy, eliminating interference, simplifying computation, or changing the distribution of learning signals. This paper proposes a general conceptual framework for enhancing large language models through deletion performed before training, during training, and after training. The framework treats deletion as a broad class of operations rather than restricting it to the removal of training examples, previously learned knowledge, or any single established technique. Potential deletion targets include data, information, parameters, architectural components, connections, internal representations, behavioral patterns, computational pathways, training objectives, auxiliary mechanisms, memory structures, and other removable objects associated with model development and operation. The framework organizes deletion along three dimensions: lifecycle stage, target category, and deletion strategy. It further introduces a formal representation of deletion operations, a target-selection principle based on expected marginal contribution, and an evaluation framework that considers capability, efficiency, reliability, generalization, and the preservation of useful functionality. A central proposition is that appropriately selected deletion operations may improve selected aspects of model performance when the benefits of removing an object exceed the costs of its removal. The paper develops a research agenda for investigating this proposition through controlled experiments, cross-stage comparisons, interaction analysis, and multi-objective evaluation. The proposed framework does not assume that deletion is inherently beneficial or that all deletion targets are technically removable. Instead, it establishes deletion as a general design dimension for systematic investigation across the lifecycle of large language models.

candidates.title: From Retrieval to Recognition:Knowledge-Enhanced Post-training of Time Series Foundation Models for Classification
candidates.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have achieved notable progress in classification tasks through large-scale pretraining. However, their post-training practice mainly focuses on implicit parameter fine-tuning, where task-relevant information is entangled with abundant irrelevant knowledge in vast parameter spaces. This may hinder TSFMs from precisely activating useful knowledge for downstream classification. To this end, we propose Retrieval-to-Recognition (R2R), a plug-and-play post-training paradigm that adapts pretrained TSFMs to time series classification. Rather than pretraining a new foundation model, R2R improves how existing TSFMs are post-trained: it introduces a decoupled query encoder to extract discriminative patterns and retrieve instance-level numerical knowledge from a constructed knowledge base. The retrieved explicit knowledge is then fused with the TSFM's implicit parametric embeddings, enabling joint knowledge transfer at both the parameter and feature levels. In this way, R2R allows TSFMs to recall task-relevant patterns learned during pretraining, improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in downstream classification transfer. Experiments on 158 time series datasets show that R2R consistently improves the classification performance of state-of-the-art TSFMs. Ablation and knowledge-enhanced studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
